newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan rulers set conditions for reform talks.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan rulers set conditions for reform talks.

text.p: Kenya's ruling party has said it will not hold talks on constitutional reforms with a non-elected opposition-backed umbrella group, local dailies reported on Thursday.

The papers quoted a statement from secretary-general of the ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) party, Joseph Kamotho, as saying the coalition National Convention Assembly (NCA), made up of human rights groups, clerics and lawyers, was a non-elective body unfit to tackle the issue of reforms.

"The issue of constitutional and legislative reforms cannot be handled haphazardly and KANU will not therefore abdicate its responsibility or delegate it to non-elective bodies like the NCA," said Kamotho.
Nine people were killed across Kenya this month after police moved in to stop rallies called by the NCA to press for constitutional reforms. Many of the parliament members were severely beaten.
A leading opposition activist, Richard Leakey, condemned Kamotho's stand and said KANU's leadership appeared unable to grasp issues of national importance.

"The statement by Kamotho demonstrates the real problem we face as Kenyans. The KANU leadership appears totally unable to grasp the issues that are of such importance to us," said Leakey, who is a member of the unregistered SAFINA party.

"It is essential for everyone to come to terms with the reality which is that in a multi-party system, the elected president has a constitutional obligation to distance himself from party politics where these impinge on the national issues."
Leakey added: "We know that Kamotho finds some concepts difficult but the peaceful transition to a real democracy that Kenyans want requires that he must."
Kamotho said parliament will be asked to enact a law to enable President Daniel arap Moi to appoint a constitutional commission to gather views of all Kenyans on the desired reforms.
On Wednesday, NCA leaders handed their agenda for talks with Moi to his office.
The NCA leaders handed over draft bills for reforms they want implemented before general elections due later this year.

The NCA is a coalition of parties, rights bodies, civic groups and churches that had united Kenya's squabbling parties in a rare show of unity in demanding reforms before presidential and parliamentary polls.
But that unity was sorely tested by Moi's agreeing to meet opposition parties this week and by KANU agreeing to some reforms last week.
No date has been set for this year's election but some opposition parties fear Moi wants to call it soon after bills are approved by parliament, where KANU has a majority.
In the coastal resort of Mombasa, organisers said a rally to press for reforms would go ahead on Saturday. Organisers said they had not sought a licence for the Saturday rally, making it illegal.
